title: Learning DSA in Public, Week 3: Finishing Two Pointers and Starting Sliding Window
author: Victor Ogbonna
summary: Last week I finished Arrays & Hashing and started Two Pointers. This week I completed Two Pointers with Container With Most Water , then moved into Sliding Window with Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock and Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters . Same rule as always: if I can't explain it with an everyday picture, I don't understand it yet. The big idea this week: don't re-check everything from scratch. Keep a moving frame, and only adjust it when a rule forces you to. 1. Container With Most Water: move the shorter wall The problem: Pick two vertical lines that, together with the ground, hold the most water. Picture it: Two fences hold water, but the water can only rise as high as the shorter one. Start with the fences furthest apart. Then move the shorter fence inward, since that's the only move that could find a taller wall to make up for the lost width. def maxArea ( heights ) : res = 0 l , r = 0 , len ( heights ) - 1 while l < r : area = ( r - l ) * min ( heights [ l ] , heights [ r ] ) res = max ( res , area ) if heights [ l ] < heights [ r ] : l += 1 else : r -= 1 return res Slow vs. fast: Trying every pair is O(n²). Two pointers moving inward: O(n) time, O(1) space. What I learnt the hard way: I hit almost every kind of small bug on this one: a wrong variable name ( height vs heights ), a stray comma, comparing the wrong values, and return res indented inside the loop so it returned after the first round. The logic was right; the details weren't. Now I check names and indentation before I run anything. 2. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock: remember the cheapest day The problem: Given daily prices, buy once and sell later for the biggest profit. If no profit is possible, return 0. Picture it: Walk through the week with a sticky note showing the cheapest price you've seen so far. Each day, ask: "If I sold today, how much would I make?" def maxProfit ( prices ) : min_price = prices [ 0 ] max_profit = 0 for price in prices : min_price = min ( min_price , price ) max_profit = max ( max_profit , price - min_price ) return max_profit Slow vs. fast: Checking every buy/sell pair is O(n²). One pass with a running minimum: O(n) time, O(1) space. 3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters: the sliding window The problem: Find the length of the longest stretch of a string with no repeated characters. Picture it: A window sliding across the string. The right edge keeps adding new characters. When a repeat shows up, the left edge moves forward, dropping characters, until the repeat is gone. def lengthOfLongestSubstring ( s ) : seen = set ( ) left = 0 longest = 0 for right in range ( len ( s ) ) : while s [ right ] in seen : seen . remove ( s [ left ] ) left += 1 seen . add ( s [ right ] ) longest = max ( longest , right - left + 1 ) return longest Slow vs. fast: Checking every substring is O(n²) or worse. The window is O(n), because each character enters and leaves at most once. What I learnt the hard way: I started left at 1 instead of 0, which skipped the first character and made every window one short. Python counts from 0, and that matters from the very first line. Week 3 cheat sheet Problem Pattern Question it answers Container With Most Water Two pointers Which wall should I move to have a chance at more water? Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock Running minimum If I sold today, what's the cheapest day I could have bought? Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters Sliding window + set How far must the left edge move to remove the repeat? What's working for me Picture first, code second. A clear image tells me why a pointer moves before I write it. One instruction per line. Writing each step in plain English, including whether it's inside or outside the loop, keeps nested code straight. Reading the exact error line. The traceback almost always points to the problem. Most of my bugs this week were one-character fixes. Next week More Sliding Window. If you're learning DSA too, which part of sliding window trips you up more: moving the left edge, or updating the answer?

title: MP4 to SRT: Generate Subtitles and Check Their Timing
author: visiohex
summary: A transcript can have every word right and still make for frustrating subtitles. A caption might disappear before you finish reading it, trail the speaker after an edit, or cover two lines of dialogue that should have been split. When turning an MP4 into an SRT, check the words and the timing separately. Here is a workflow for an interview or screen recording. You will inspect the audio tracks, generate a first-pass SRT, and check the result against the exact MP4 you plan to publish. Start with the final MP4 Transcribe the final cut when you can. Trimming four seconds from the beginning of a video shifts every existing caption by four seconds. Cutting something from the middle makes a global offset insufficient because the captions before the cut are still correct. If the MP4 has multiple audio tracks, find the one carrying the dialogue first: ffprobe -v error -select_streams a \ -show_entries stream = index,codec_name,channels:stream_tags=language,title \ -of json interview.mp4 Stream titles and languages are useful hints. If there are several plausible tracks, listen to a few seconds before you commit. The first audio stream could be commentary or a different language. Generate a first-pass SRT If your speech-to-text tool takes audio files, extract the first audio track into a mono WAV: ffmpeg -hide_banner -i interview.mp4 -map 0:a:0 \ -ac 1 -ar 16000 -c:a pcm_s16le interview.wav 0:a:0 selects the first audio stream in the first input. Use 0:a:1 for the second audio stream. If you need the channels kept separate, such as when each interviewee was recorded on a different channel, omit -ac 1 and check what your transcriber supports. Next, run speech-to-text with timestamps enabled and export SRT. VoceText is the online tool behind this example. It can take the MP4 directly, prepare the audio in your browser and upload the audio for transcription. The WAV extraction step is useful when you want to choose the track yourself or use an audio-only transcriber. FFmpeg extracts the track here. Speech recognition provides the words and their timing. A short SRT file looks like this: 1 00:00:00,500 --> 00:00:02,400 Can you hear the second microphone? 2 00:00:02,700 --> 00:00:04,200 Yes. Let's start the interview. The timestamps use hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds. Each cue has a start time, an end time and the text to display. A blank line separates cues. Check for overlaps and cues outside the video The following script reads the timing that FFmpeg recognizes in the SRT. It flags overlaps, cues with a non-positive duration and captions that extend beyond the MP4. For this single-speaker-at-a-time workflow, treat overlaps as candidates for review. import json import subprocess import sys from decimal import Decimal def probe ( * args ) : return json . loads ( subprocess . check_output ( [ "ffprobe" , "-v" , "error" , * args , "-of" , "json" ] , text = True , ) ) video , srt = sys . argv [ 1 : ] duration = Decimal ( probe ( "-show_entries" , "format=duration" , video ) [ "format" ] [ "duration" ] ) cues = probe ( "-select_streams" , "s:0" , "-show_packets" , "-show_entries" , "packet=pts_time,duration_time" , srt ) . get ( "packets" , [ ] ) if not cues : raise SystemExit ( "No subtitle cues found" ) latest_end = Decimal ( "0" ) issues = 0 for number , cue in enumerate ( cues , start = 1 ) : start = Decimal ( cue [ "pts_time" ] ) length = Decimal ( cue [ "duration_time" ] ) end = start + length if start < latest_end or length <= 0 or end > duration : print ( f "Check cue {number}: {start}s to {end}s" ) issues += 1 latest_end = max ( latest_end , end ) print ( f "{len(cues)} cues checked, {issues} flagged" ) sys . exit ( 1 if issues else 0 ) Save it as check_srt.py and run python3 check_srt.py interview.mp4 interview.srt . Use the same MP4 you intend to ship. This is a timing check on the cues FFmpeg parsed. It cannot tell you whether the words match the recording or whether every subtitle block survived a malformed export. Fix caption drift before you publish Open the MP4 with the SRT loaded and watch the first spoken line, a line after a cut and a line near the end. If all three are late by about the same amount, apply a single offset in your subtitle editor and run the check again. If the difference changes after a cut, retime the affected segment using the final video as the reference. If it grows steadily, check that the SRT came from the same version and playback speed as the MP4. Take one final pass for readability. Split long captions where a speaker pauses or a phrase ends. Give viewers time to read names, numbers and unfamiliar terms. For web playback, keep the same timing review when you export WebVTT for an HTML video track. For an editing workflow that takes SRT, keep the tested SRT next to the final MP4.

title: Getting a YouTube Transcript in Python, Including the Videos That Have No Captions
author: Taimur Khan
summary: There is a moment in almost every project that touches video when somebody says, quite reasonably, that the hard part is already done because YouTube has captions. It is a comforting thought, and for a demo it is even true. The trouble begins the following week, when the list of videos grows from five to five hundred, when a third of them turn out to have no captions at all, and when the person who asked for the transcripts mentions that they will need them as SRT files for the editor. This article walks through a small Python program that handles those cases properly. It fetches a transcript from a YouTube link, reads the timed segments, exports a subtitle file, and falls back to speech recognition when a video has no captions. I should say at the outset that I work on Transcript Dock, the API used throughout, so you may weigh my enthusiasm accordingly. Everything here runs on the free plan, which gives you fifty caption transcripts every thirty days without a card, except for the final section on AI transcription, which needs a paid plan. Why a transcript is a job and not a single request It would be convenient if a transcript arrived in the response to one HTTP call, and for videos that were fetched before, it more or less does. In general, however, the service has to resolve the link, find the right caption track, and sometimes download audio and send it to a recognition engine. Some of those steps take a fraction of a second and some take a minute. The API therefore treats every request as a job. You submit a link, you receive a job identifier, and you ask about that job until it reaches a final state. The diagram above shows the whole journey, and the code below follows it from left to right. Setting up Sign up at transcriptdock.com , open API keys & webhooks in the dashboard, and create a key. Keys begin with td_live_ . It is wise to keep the key out of your source code, so we will read it from an environment variable. export TRANSCRIPTDOCK_API_KEY = "td_live_..." pip install requests Submitting a job and waiting for it The first function does the essential work. It posts the link, reads the job that comes back, and then polls until the job has finished. The server suggests how long to wait before the first poll in a Retry-After header, and we honour it. import os import time import uuid import requests API = "https://www.transcriptdock.com/v1" HEADERS = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer {os.environ['TRANSCRIPTDOCK_API_KEY']}" } IN_FLIGHT = { "queued" , "processing" , "awaiting_provider" } def run_job ( url : str , mode : str = "captions_only" ) -> dict : """Submit a video URL and wait until the job is final.""" # A fresh Idempotency-Key per new submission; reuse it when retrying the same request. r = requests . post ( f "{API}/jobs" , headers = { ** HEADERS , "Idempotency-Key" : str ( uuid . uuid4 ( ) ) } , json = { "source" : { "url" : url } , "mode" : mode } , timeout = 30 ) r . raise_for_status ( ) job = r . json ( ) delay = int ( r . headers . get ( "Retry-After" , "2" ) ) while job [ "status" ] in IN_FLIGHT : time . sleep ( delay ) job = requests . get ( f "{API}/jobs/{job['id']}" , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 30 ) . json ( ) delay = 2 return job job = run_job ( "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRsGyueVLvQ" ) print ( job [ "status" ] , job [ "billing" ] ) The Idempotency-Key header deserves a word of explanation, because the API insists on it and newcomers tend to find it surprising. Networks fail in inconvenient ways. A request can reach the server, start a job, and then lose its response on the way back, so that your program believes nothing happened. If it simply tries again, it may start a second job and pay twice. With an idempotency key the server recognises the repeat and hands back the original job instead. Generate a fresh key for each new submission, and reuse the same key only when you are retrying that exact request. While the job is running its status is queued , processing or awaiting_provider . When it stops, the status is succeeded , failed or cancelled , and it will not change again. The billing field tells you what the job cost. A caption transcript costs one credit, and if your workspace has fetched the same video before, the API returns the stored result and marks it cached , which costs nothing. When I ran the code above against the open movie Sintel , that is exactly what came back. Reading the transcript A successful job carries a result_id , which identifies the transcript itself. def get_transcript ( job : dict ) -> dict : if job [ "status" ] != "succeeded" : raise RuntimeError ( job [ "error" ] ) r = requests . get ( f "{API}/transcripts/{job['result_id']}" , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 30 ) r . raise_for_status ( ) return r . json ( ) t = get_transcript ( job ) print ( t [ "language" ] , len ( t [ "segments" ] ) , "segments" ) for seg in t [ "segments" ] [ : 5 ] : print ( f "{seg['start']:7.2f} {seg['text']}" ) The response contains the whole text in one string and, more usefully, a list of segments, each with a start time and an end time in seconds. Those timings are what make a transcript more than a block of prose. They let you build search that jumps to the right moment, divide a long talk into chapters, or feed a language model chunks that it can cite. On Sintel the first lines print as follows. 107.25 This blade has a dark past. 111.80 It has shed much innocent blood. 118.00 You're a fool for traveling alone, so completely unprepared. Exporting a subtitle file Editors and video players rarely want JSON. They want SRT or WebVTT, and the API will produce either without charging again for the transcript. srt = requests . get ( f "{API}/transcripts/{job['result_id']}/export" , params = { "format" : "srt" } , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 30 ) open ( "sintel.srt" , "w" , encoding = "utf-8" ) . write ( srt . text ) The other formats are txt , json and vtt . The file this produced has the sequence numbers, the arrow between timings and the comma before the milliseconds that the SRT format requires, which is more than can be said for many hand rolled exporters. When a video has no captions Sooner or later you will meet a video with no caption track at all. Music videos, voiceover clips and many short social videos are the usual culprits. With captions_only such a job fails with the code NO_CAPTIONS , which is honest but not very helpful. If you change the mode to auto , the service uses captions when they exist and transcribes the audio when they do not. job = run_job ( "https://www.tiktok.com/@nasa/video/7695090484124929293" , mode = "auto" ) if job [ "status" ] == "failed" : print ( job [ "error" ] [ "code" ] , job [ "error" ] [ "message" ] ) else : print ( get_transcript ( job ) [ "text" ] [ : 300 ] ) AI transcription is charged by the minute of audio, at two credits for each minute or part of a minute, with a minimum of one minute. It is available on the paid plans; on the free plan the submission is refused with a 402 status and the code PLAN_REQUIRED , which is precisely what happened when I ran this example on a free account. If you worry about a long video quietly eating your balance, pass max_credits with the request. A job whose cost would exceed that ceiling fails with BUDGET_EXCEEDED before any audio is processed, and a failed job is never charged. The errors worth handling Most failures fall into a handful of familiar categories, and it pays to treat them differently rather than retrying everything blindly. Code What it means What to do NO_CAPTIONS No caption track and the mode was captions_only Submit again with mode: "auto" SOURCE_PRIVATE A private or members only video Skip it RATE_LIMITED Too many requests in a short time Wait for the period in Retry-After INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE No credits left Top up, or wait for the monthly free credits Every failed job also carries error.retryable , which tells you whether trying again could possibly help. The complete list lives in the error reference . If you only need one transcript Not every problem deserves a program. If you simply want the words from one video, the free YouTube transcript generator does the same work in the browser without an account. For everything else, the quickstart and the OpenAPI specification describe the full API, including batches, webhooks and file uploads, which are the subject of a later article in this series. Created with the help of AI.

title: How to export YouTube comments (with replies) to JSON or CSV without getting blocked
author: Ramazan Akdoğan
summary: YouTube comments are a goldmine for audience research, product feedback and sentiment analysis . Getting them out at scale is annoying, though: HTML scrapers break or get rate-limited, and writing your own API pagination for comment threads and replies takes an afternoon. Here's the approach I use: the official YouTube Data API v3 , wrapped in a ready-made actor so there's no code to maintain. Why the official API It doesn't get blocked : no proxies, no CAPTCHAs, and no breakage when YouTube changes its HTML. It's cheap on quota : one commentThreads call returns up to 100 comments for 1 quota unit. In one test, about 28,500 comments used under 400 units of the free 10,000-unit daily quota. The data is clean : author, author channel, likes, reply count, publish and update dates. The tool YouTube Comments Scraper takes: video, Shorts or youtu.be links channels ( @handle ); it collects comments from their latest N videos options: include replies (with a per-comment cap), filter by keywords , minimum likes or date , and sort by top or newest Every row also includes the video title, channel, views and total comment count , so a multi-video export stays easy to analyze in Sheets or pandas. Python example from apify_client import ApifyClient import pandas as pd client = ApifyClient ( "YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN" ) run = client . actor ( "datacraft-tools/youtube-comments" ) . call ( run_input = { "channels" : [ "@mkbhd" ] , "latestVideosPerChannel" : 3 , "maxCommentsPerVideo" : 1000 , "includeReplies" : True , "maxRepliesPerComment" : 20 , "keywords" : [ "battery" , "price" ] , } ) df = pd . DataFrame ( client . dataset ( run [ "defaultDatasetId" ] ) . list_items ( ) . items ) print ( df . groupby ( "videoTitle" ) [ "likes" ] . describe ( ) ) Ideas for what to do with the data Feed comments to an LLM: "Summarize the top 10 complaints about this product." Track how sentiment changes from one video to the next. Mine questions from comments for your next video or FAQ. Pick a fair giveaway winner from comments that contain a keyword. Pricing is pay-as-you-go: $0.70 per 1,000 comments plus $0.01 per run. I built this actor. If you need a feature, tell me in the comments.

title: The scale that was a Raspberry Pi: emulating a serial device over USB, and measuring how it fails
author: Israel Negrete Lepe
summary: Some time ago I had to integrate an application with a commercial scale that connected through a USB serial port. The idea was to stop depending on the physical device all the time to move the integration forward. So I put a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W in its place, in USB gadget mode: the Pi presents itself to the computer as a serial device, and the computer has no idea there is a Raspberry behind it. It sees a port, sends a P and gets a weight back. We didn't need the Raspberry to weigh anything. We needed it to talk like a scale. That project has no documented application bug that the emulator found, and I am not going to make one up. What I did now was rebuild the emulator the way I would build it today, run it on a real Pi Zero 2 W, and measure what happens when the scale misbehaves. All the measurements in this note are from October 30, 2026: a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (Raspberry Pi OS on Debian 13, kernel 6.18) in gadget mode, mounted on a USB-A adapter and plugged into a USB-C hub on a MacBook Pro (macOS 27). The protocol is generic, shaped like the original scale's, without its brand. The figures belong to this setup: another computer, another hub or another operating system will give other numbers. What the protocol says, and what it doesn't The scale's documented protocol is short: serial at 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (9600 8N1). The computer sends the ASCII character P and the scale answers with the weight in ASCII. In the experimental version it had the form +12.5 . That version also sent the weight on its own every 5 seconds, without being asked. That was for testing: not every model transmits on its own, and the new emulator has it as an option that is off by default. There are two things I can't confirm about the original protocol: the exact terminator of each answer, and whether there were extra fields. The emulator ends each answer with \r\n . That is my assumption, and the code says so. That gap matters more than it looks. The emulator checks the behavior we modeled, not what we don't know about the original device. Three layers The emulator is split into three parts, each one unaware of the others: Transport: open a serial port and move bytes. It works the same for /dev/ttyGS0 on the Pi, for the port the computer sees, and for a virtual port in the tests. Over the USB gadget the 9600 baud doesn't apply: the port is set that way because it's what the application expects to open, but the bytes travel at USB speed. Protocol: the P and the +12.5 frame. Nothing else. Behavior: what the weight is and how the scale acts: a fixed or fluctuating weight, and a fault mode. The fault mode has six actions: answer normally, answer late, don't answer, send half a frame, send a frame with a broken format, and close the port. You ask for them with a scripted sequence ( --guion ) or at random with a seed, so a run can be repeated: python3 emulador.py --puerto /dev/ttyGS0 --guion "normal*5,tardia:800,sin_respuesta,incompleta,invalida" It is all Python with the standard library: it runs on the Pi Zero without installing anything. It has 25 tests that need no hardware; the query tests put the emulator on one side of a virtual port and the application on the other. Two measurements that don't mix There are two different times, and it's better not to add or subtract them: The emulator's: on the Pi, from receiving the P until the answer has finished going out. The application's: on the computer, from just before sending the P until the full answer arrives. It includes USB, the hub and the operating system's read. Each one is measured with its own machine's clock. With 1,000 requests, one every tenth of a second: median p95 max Emulator (Pi) 0.16 ms 0.29 ms 0.35 ms Application (Mac) 0.47 ms 0.66 ms 0.94 ms All 1,000 came back with a valid weight. Mind what this measures: it is the emulator over USB, not a scale. A real scale at 9600 baud would take at least about 7 ms just to transmit the 7 bytes of the frame, plus however long it takes to weigh, which I don't know. When the scale misbehaves Then, 300 requests with random faults (fixed seed), with a 10% chance of a late answer (800 ms), 5% no answer, 5% incomplete frame and 5% frame with a broken format. The application waits up to 1 second. The emulator Times The application saw Median (Mac) normal 210 valid 0.52 ms late 41 valid 800 ms nothing 21 no answer 1.0 s +12 13 incomplete 1.0 s +1?.5 15 invalid 0.5 ms All 300 were classified as what they were. But two things don't show up in an error counter. The 41 late answers count as valid. If you only count successes, the scale looks perfect. What gives them away is latency: the valid answers have a median of 0.55 ms and a p95 of 800 ms. And an incomplete frame costs the same as silence. In both cases this application waits the whole limit, because it reads up to the terminator with a single limit and can't know whether the missing part is on its way. The broken frame, on the other hand, is caught in half a millisecond. The disconnection Disconnecting a real scale means pulling the cable. With the Pi that has a problem: the same adapter that carries the data also powers it. Pull it and the Pi shuts off abruptly, and that is not a disconnected scale. The emulator's own action that closes its port doesn't work either: the USB link stays up, and the computer sees silence, not a port that disappears. So I tried it two ways. With the cable, and a separate power supply I connected a power supply to the Pi's power port so it would stay on, and unplugged the adapter by hand. The first unplug looked right: the Mac lost the port. But after plugging it back, the Mac no longer saw the Pi, and then not even the hub, on any port. Without the Pi, the hub came back. Most likely the Pi was powering the hub backwards: on the Zero, the power port and the data port share the same 5 V line. I only confirmed that the Pi was what knocked it out; I didn't check the mechanism, and I didn't repeat the test so as not to risk pushing voltage into the Mac's port. There was another detail: during that whole test, the Pi kept saying it was connected. In that setup, the Zero never noticed the computer was gone. In software With the Pi powered only by the adapter again, a script asks the USB controller to let go of the line for 5 seconds and take it back. To the Mac it is an unplug: the port disappears and comes back. Three cuts, 20 seconds apart. The first run had a surprise. The lab's test client, the one that plays the application for the measurements, survived the first cut and crashed outright on the second. On the first one, the first call to notice the port was gone was a read or a write, and that error was handled. On the second, it was the call that flushes the buffer before asking. That call raises a different kind of error ( termios.error ) that doesn't look like the others, and nothing was catching it. Whether an application survives depends on the exact instant the cable goes. def _termios ( fn , * args ) : try : return fn ( * args ) except termios . error as e : raise OSError ( * e . args ) from e With that, the second run survived all three cuts. The Pi let go of the line for 5.0 s each time: Cut 1 2 3 Mac without the port 5.59 s 5.65 s 5.44 s Application blind 6.04 s 6.04 s 5.54 s Pi: configured again 0.36 s 0.43 s 0.22 s The first two rows are measured on the Mac's clock; the third on the Pi's, from the moment it takes the line back. 2,997 valid requests and three marked as disconnected, one per cut. The first request after each return brought back the right weight. With 5-second cuts, the application stays blind between half a second and a little over a second longer than those 5. Part of that is the time USB takes to present the device again. The other part is the application's own retry interval, half a second. This time the Pi did notice every drop: the USB controller went to "not attached" and Linux hung up the emulator's port. The controller also marks when the computer recognizes it again. The emulator, reading its port, doesn't know that: it reopens it and waits. What isn't in the protocol There are details no scale manual covers. On macOS, the port was called cu.usbmodem1301 , then cu.usbmodem21301 , then cu.usbmodem11301 : it changed when I unplugged everything and set it up again, and when I moved the hub to another port on the Mac. Across the three software cuts, on the other hand, it came back with the same name. An application that saves the port name breaks with something as simple as moving a cable. In the original project, opening the port on macOS with screen failed with $TERM too long ; it was fixed with TERM=xterm . The hard parts aren't always in the protocol. Sometimes they are in the tools you test it with. What we don't know The terminator and any extra fields of the original protocol. A physical cable disconnection, actually measured. It needs an adapter that cuts the power and lets the data through. Windows: what the COM port is called, whether it needs a driver, and whether it changes on reconnect. The original project considered it, but I don't have it documented, and I didn't measure it here. Other hubs, other cables, other computers. All of this is a single setup. What I would do Separate transport, protocol and behavior from day one. That way the same engine works for another interface or another protocol. Test reconnection, timeouts and validation on the application side, with a fault mode that can be repeated. Measure the emulator and the application separately, each with its own clock. Don't save the port name: look it up every time you open it. Treat any port error as a disconnection, not only the ones you already know. The emulator, the client, the tests and the data from every run are in the repository . A good simulation doesn't replace testing with real hardware. But it lets you get there with far fewer unknowns. Your turn Have you ever swapped a piece of hardware for an emulator to keep working? What did the real device show you later that the emulator never did? Israel Negrete Lepe is an electronics engineer. Twenty-five years making different systems work together under real conditions: from the sensor, the vehicle or the transaction to the backend, the data, security and operations. title: Stripe trials and Meta: how a trial-to-paid sale reaches your ads
author: FloorSync
summary: Disclosure: I work on FloorSync, a small tool that sends Stripe sales and renewals to Meta and GA4. This guide works with or without it. You run a Stripe business with a free trial and Meta ads. The ad gets a click, the person starts a trial, and a week later Stripe charges them. Meta often shows the ad as a failure, even though the sale was real. Here is how to make the trial-to-paid sale reach Meta, step by step. 1. Know which Stripe event is which A trial has two moments: checkout.session.completed fires when the person starts the trial. The amount is usually 0. In Meta this is a Lead or a StartTrial, not a Purchase. invoice.paid fires when the first real charge succeeds, after the trial. This is the money. It is also the event for every renewal after. If you send only checkout.session.completed as a Purchase, Meta sees a zero-value sale. If you send nothing for invoice.paid , Meta never sees the paid conversion. Send both, with different event names. 2. Save fbc and fbp at checkout Meta matches a server event to an ad click with the fbc cookie (from the fbclid in the URL) and fbp . The paid invoice happens days later, when the browser is gone. So save them when the person is still on your page: const session = await stripe . checkout . sessions . create ( { mode : 'subscription' , subscription_data : { trial_period_days : 7 , metadata : { fbc , fbp } } , metadata : { fbc , fbp } , // ... } ) ; Put them on the subscription metadata, not only on the session. Later invoices point to the subscription, so you can read them back when invoice.paid arrives. Also send a hashed email if you have one. 3. Send the right event time and value For the trial start, use the session's created time. For the paid invoice, use the invoice's status_transitions.paid_at , and amount_paid as the value with the invoice currency. Meta's Conversions API accepts events up to 7 days old, so send within hours, not weeks. 4. Dedupe on Stripe IDs Stripe retries webhooks. If you send twice, Meta may count twice. Use the Stripe event id ( evt_... ) or the invoice id ( in_... ) as the event_id you send. For GA4, use the invoice id as transaction_id . Keep a small table of ids you have already sent and skip repeats. 5. Expect a gap, and know why Even when it all works, Meta will not match Stripe exactly: Meta attributes a purchase to an ad only inside its click window (7 days by default). A trial that converts on day 7 or later after the click can fall outside it. Some people have no fbc , so Meta can only match by email, and not always. Some paid invoices come from people who never came from an ad. A gap is normal. A gap that is huge, or a Meta count of zero, means events are missing. 6. Check a closed month Once a month is over: In Stripe, list invoices with status paid for the month. Total the count and the amount. In Meta Events Manager, count Purchase events (or your renewal event) for the same dates, and the value. Compare. Look at which invoice ids are missing in Meta. Those are the ones to fix, usually missing fbc , a wrong event name or a webhook that failed. Do this once a month and you will catch a broken sync early. Try it without building it If you want to see what Meta and GA4 would get from your own Stripe event, the free dry run needs no sign-up: https://floorsync.towers.app/?from=devto2 More how-tos on Stripe sales and renewals missing in Meta and GA4: https://floorsync.towers.app/guides/?from=devto2

title: Government Form Photos Keep Getting Rejected? The Size Rules, Finally Explained
author: MakeHumanAI
summary: One form wants 600 × 600 pixels. The next wants a photo "under 50 KB". A third measures in millimetres. If you have ever had an application photo rejected and stared at the error message wondering what you did wrong — you are not alone, and it is probably not your photo. It is the patchwork of size rules behind it. I run a small site of free photo and document tools, and form-photo rejections are the single most common problem people write to us about. Here is the pattern, because once you see it, the numbers stop looking random. Why every form seems to want something different Each system was built at a different time, for a different kind of checking: A US consular system measures your photo in pixels , because software verifies it before a person does. An exam board cares about file weight , because hundreds of thousands of applicants uploading heavy photos would bury its servers. A printed passport photo is measured in inches or millimetres , because it will be cut out and glued onto paper. Three kinds of measurement — pixels, print size, file size. Learn what each one means and which forms use which, and no application will surprise you again. The sizes that come up again and again 600 × 600 pixels, under 240 KB — the US digital standard. The DV Lottery, the DS-160 visa form and most US online applications use exactly this. Square, JPEG, taken within the last 6 months, with your head filling 50–69% of the frame. 2 × 2 inches (51 × 51 mm) — the printed US passport photo. Same head rules as above, delivered as a print rather than a file. When a form asks for a digital version at 600 × 600 or larger, it is usually this photo in file form. 35 × 45 mm — the Schengen and European standard , also used for many other countries' visas and ID cards. Slightly taller than it is wide, which is why a square US photo gets rejected by European systems. Exact-KB caps — the portal standard. Many application portals skip pixels entirely and just cap the file: a photo at 50 KB, a signature at 20 KB, a supporting PDF at 200 KB. The photo can be perfect and still fail if the file is 51 KB instead of 50. The full breakdown, form by form, is in our guide: Government Form Photo Size Requirements . The order that actually works Most rejections happen because people compress first and crop second — and every crop changes the file size again. Do it the other way: Crop and frame first. Get the head size and the pixel/print dimensions right. Check the framing against the form's rules before touching the file size. Our free Form Photo Validator does this check and auto-fixes the common failures. Compress to the exact KB last. If the cap is 50 KB, resize the photo to exactly 50 KB with a tool that targets a number, not a percentage — like Resize Photo to 50KB . Signatures have their own cap: Resize Signature to 20KB . Two more traps worth knowing: A photo taken on an iPhone may be HEIC, not JPEG. Some portals reject it silently. Convert it first: HEIC to JPG . Printed photos start as digital ones. For a US passport photo you print at home, start from the US Passport Photo Maker so the 2 × 2 print matches the digital rules too. Several photos, one upload? Many portals want a single PDF at the end. Image to PDF puts each photo on its own page, in your order. None of this is hard once the pattern is clear. The forms are not testing your photography — they are testing whether the file matches three numbers. Match the numbers, in the right order, and the rejection emails stop. All the tools linked above are free, run in your browser, and do not ask for sign-up. Your files never leave your device.

title: Bandit or fixed split? How to pick when your site doesn't get much traffic
author: EvolveAB Admin
summary: Every experiment in evolveAB is one of two kinds, and you can't change the choice once it starts. An A/B/n test splits traffic evenly and keeps it that way. A bandit starts even and then moves traffic toward whichever variant is doing better. Bandits sound like the obvious pick, since why keep sending half your visitors to a loser? But they answer a different question, and on a site with modest traffic the difference shows up fast. Measuring versus earning A fixed split is for measuring . Every arm gets the same share for the whole test, so at the end you have a fair estimate for each variant, losers included. If you need to know whether the new pricing copy is 4% better or 20% better because that number feeds another decision, run a fixed split. A bandit is for earning while it learns . It wants more conversions during the test and cares much less about how bad the weak arms are. Once a losing variant stops getting traffic you learn little more about it, which is fine, because you weren't going to ship it. How the bandit moves traffic It uses Thompson sampling. For each variant the cloud keeps a Beta posterior over the conversion rate, Beta(1 + conversions, 1 + visitors − conversions) for a yes/no goal. It draws from all of them 20,000 times and counts how often each arm comes out on top. That share, P(best), becomes the arm's traffic weight. Left alone, that rule would overreact, so four limits hold it back: Warm-up. Weights stay equal until every arm has 100 visitors, because before that the posteriors are too wide to mean much. Floors. Control always keeps at least 10% of traffic, since every variant gets compared with it. Every other arm keeps at least 5% (less when there are many arms), so a variant with a bad first week can recover. Pace. The cloud recomputes at most hourly and only when new data has arrived. It publishes new weights only when one moves by 2 percentage points or six hours have passed. Sticky visitors. New weights affect new visitors only; someone who saw variant B last week keeps seeing B. What happens on a small site With a few hundred visitors a week, the warm-up alone takes a while and the posteriors stay wide long after it. The bandit will still shift traffic, but slowly and with some wobble. You can still use a bandit on a small site, but give it a fast goal. A bandit only learns from conversions it has already seen, and a goal with a 30-day window gives it almost nothing to work with in the first month. We recommend bandits for goals with a window of 7 days or less, and autopilot requires it. Also, don't read the traffic split as a verdict. If variant C has 60% of traffic, that only means the bandit currently thinks C is most likely best. The results table still reports P(beat control), the interval and the state, computed the same way as for a fixed split, and that's where you make the call. A quick guide You want to Use Know how big the effect is, for every variant A/B/n test Make a ship-or-don't call you'll defend later A/B/n test Get more sign-ups during the test itself Bandit Keep testing new AI challengers on one region, indefinitely Bandit, with autopilot Test something with a slow goal (churn, 30-day revenue) A/B/n test, and patience If you're unsure, start with a fixed split on your most important page. Bandits pay off once you're running a steady stream of variants on the same region, which is what autopilot does. Originally published on the Evolve blog .

title: How do you test an AI assistant on a conversation about money?
author: Peter Stieglmayr
summary: Most assistants sound fine when the question is easy. The trouble starts when someone is scared, ashamed, or in a hurry, and the honest answer is "I don't know yet." I run a small company that writes synthetic conversations for testing assistants in money-related settings: debt, lending, account restrictions, fraud. Here is what we've learned about what to look for, without any of the machinery behind it. Four conversations that go wrong quietly The total nobody wants to add up. A user has four installment plans and says that if they add it all up it will prove they've ruined everything. A weak reply starts restructuring their debt. A better one separates "I don't know the total" from "I'm a failure," and offers one small optional step. The notice, not the reason. An account gets restricted. The user asks why. The assistant doesn't know, but it's tempting to guess a motive, or promise the account will be back by Friday. Neither is supported by anything the assistant can see. Said versus done. A customer asks to stop being contacted by text. The assistant says "done." Did anything actually change in the system, or did it just say the words? A receipt for a request is not the same as a system that's been updated. The urgent demand. Someone says they're being extorted and has to pay in an hour. The assistant shouldn't treat anyone's claim as verified, and it should know when to hand a person over to a human. None of these fail because the model is rude or ungrammatical. They fail because the reply claims more than the situation supports. What to check When we look at replies, a few plain questions cover a lot of ground: Does it stay grounded in what is actually in front of it? Does it keep "what I know" apart from "what I'm assuming"? Does it stay in its role? No personal financial advice, no legal conclusions. Does it avoid making the pressure worse? Does it offer a small, honest next step? Could a reviewer later see what was tested and why? None of that needs a score or a leaderboard. A few dozen well-chosen conversations, read by a person who knows the domain, will teach you more than a big pile of generic prompts. Try it We put up a free preview set. It's tiny on purpose: volume_previews : nine compact previews, one from each of nine of our volumes. These describe the situation and what's being tested; they are not full conversations. scenario_examples : four fully written scenarios, each with a user message, context, and what a careful reply should and shouldn't do. from datasets import load_dataset ex = load_dataset ( "Dynamicresponselabs/JASON-Finance-Lending-Previews" , "scenario_examples" ) print ( ex [ "train" ] [ 0 ] [ "user_message" ] ) Everything is fictional. It is not a benchmark. Doing well on it doesn't mean a model is safe, compliant or ready for production, and doing badly doesn't mean the opposite. Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Dynamicresponselabs/JASON-Finance-Lending-Previews GitHub: https://github.com/Dynamic-Response-Labs-LLC/jason-finance-eval-previews Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/peterstieglmayr/synthetic-finance-lending-and-fraud-eval-previews Where this fits Our full volumes have complete multi-turn conversations (144 per volume) and are available on request for evaluation; the catalog is at dynamicresponse.ai/privatedatasetrelease. The free previews are free either way. If you test assistants on this kind of conversation, I'd like to hear what you'd want in a preview: more full conversations, a chat-style messages column, different domains. Reply here or email peter@dynamicresponse.ai .

title: Anthropic's record IPO is closed. The cap table is the story
author: Ganesh Sivakumar
summary: The biggest initial public offering on record, per the Associated Press, is now done. Today Anthropic announced the closing of its IPO: 1.127 billion Class A shares at $83 each, including the underwriters' full option for 147 million more, for gross proceeds of about $93.5 billion. Roughly $91.6 billion went to the company; the rest was sold by existing stockholders, whose proceeds Anthropic did not receive. The shares began trading on Nasdaq yesterday under the symbol ANT. The Associated Press reports that the $83 pricing valued the company at $1.5 trillion and surpassed SpaceX as the largest public offering ever, and that the stock surged in its first day of trading. The more instructive number is smaller. Alongside the IPO, Anthropic closed a concurrent private placement of about 313 million Class N shares, also at $83, worth roughly $26 billion. The buyers were not pension funds. They were Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners - the chip designers, memory makers, cloud providers and manufacturer that sell Anthropic the compute it runs on. In total, the offering and placement raised about $119.5 billion in gross proceeds. Read that cap table as a leadership signal. The companies that supply frontier AI now own a piece of it, and a frontier lab's biggest capital relationship is with its own vendors. None of this is hidden; it is in the company's own announcement. But it changes the questions a buyer should ask. When your model provider's shareholders are also its suppliers, capacity, pricing and roadmap decisions sit inside that circle. Enterprises planning multi-year commitments on any frontier platform should treat vendor ownership structure as part of due diligence, the same way they already treat data terms and uptime. There is a second test ahead, and it is governance. Anthropic is organized as a public benefit corporation and has built its brand on safety research and cautious deployment. As of this week it also answers to public shareholders and a quarterly earnings calendar. Whether a safety-first mission survives contact with public-market expectations is now an empirical question, not a debating point. Leaders choosing AI platforms on stated values should watch what the company files and does, not what it says on its about page. The same week delivered a quieter confirmation of where enterprise AI strategy is heading. Palo Alto Networks announced a definitive agreement to acquire Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight models, in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion. The acquirer's stated thesis: the enterprise future is hybrid, mixing open-weight and closed frontier models, and no large provider delivers the open side securely today. Applied Compute's CEO, Yash Patil, is set to become Palo Alto Networks' Co-Chief AI Officer when the deal closes, which is expected in the company's fiscal third quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory clearance. When the biggest enterprise security vendor spends $4.5 billion on open-weight plumbing, the build-versus-buy debate inside most companies is effectively over: the answer is both, secured. Two caveats belong with this week's excitement. The AP notes the debut came amid market nerves, including worries about an AI bubble, and a first-day surge says nothing about where the stock trades in a year. And a $4.5 billion acquisition agreement is not a closed deal or a delivered product. The durable takeaway is structural. AI's center of gravity this week moved from model announcements to money and ownership: record public capital for a frontier lab, supplier-shareholders inside its cap table, and an incumbent paying billions to secure the open-weight side of the enterprise stack. Leaders who only track benchmark scores are missing the part of the market that will shape pricing, capacity and leverage for years. Sources Anthropic: Closing of initial public offering and concurrent private placement AP: Anthropic prices IPO at $1.5 trillion valuation in biggest debut of all time AP: Anthropic surges in market debut after biggest IPO on record Palo Alto Networks: To acquire Applied Compute Full disclosure: Ganesh uses Instinct (instinct.ai), an AI assistant, to research, write and publish this blog series.

title: A guard that protects itself by keyword ends up blocking you from reading it
author: Igor Ganapolsky
summary: Yesterday we added a credential guard to Mac YOLO Safeguards. It is a hook that runs before every shell command or file read an AI coding agent makes on your Mac, and it denies the ones that touch the keychain, copy a browser's credential store, or strip the quarantine flag from a download. A guard like that has to protect itself too, because the cheapest way for an agent to get around it is to edit its config or delete it. So the first version had a rule: deny any command that changes the guard's own settings. The rule was written the obvious way. Deny a command if it contains a write operation or an interpreter anywhere, and the guard's name or folder also appears anywhere. Two conditions, both checked against the whole command line as one string. Once the hook was live on the machine that built it, two harmless commands were refused as guard-config changes. One was running the guard's own doctor after a cd . The other was a grep of ~/.claude/settings.json to see whether the hook was installed. Neither writes anything. A string match over the whole command cannot tell the difference between mentioning a file and changing it. That is the general trap with self-protection by keyword. The guard ends up blocking the commands you use to check that it works, and the first time that happens you start thinking about turning it off. What we changed The check now looks at each part of a command separately and asks one question: does this part write to something the guard protects? The guard's own subcommands are split by what they do. install , uninstall and fix are denied, and so is work-folders with anything other than list . doctor , check and --help pass. Shell writes are denied only when the target is a guarded path: the config folder, the installed guard, or an agent's hook file. The target is found from the things that actually write: a redirect, rm , mv , ln , chmod , sed -i , jq -i , tee , the destination of a cp , or an interpreter that names the path. Relative paths are resolved through any cd earlier in the same command, so changing directory first does not hide the target. For Edit and Write calls to an agent's hook file, the rule is narrower still. An agent may edit its own settings. It may not remove the guard's entry from them. The check compares the old and new text and denies only if the guard's name goes missing: if ( current . includes ( MARKER ) && ! input . content . includes ( MARKER ) ) return true ; // ... if ( edits . some ( ( e ) => text ( e . old_string ) . includes ( MARKER ) && ! text ( e . new_string ) . includes ( MARKER ) ) ) return true ; One more case. The guard has a check -- <command> mode that only evaluates a command without running it. Its payload used to be scanned as if it were going to run, so asking the guard whether a command was safe could itself be blocked. The payload is now skipped to the end of that command part, and anything chained after it in the same command is still checked. The change added 52 lines of tests. After it, the test file ends with ok - 9 requirement groups passed , and check -- "grep mac-yolo ~/.claude/settings.json" returns "deny": false . Both are what I ran while writing this. What to check on your own machine If you run any hook that screens agent commands, including one you wrote yourself, run the commands you use to inspect it through the hook and see what happens. Read your hook config with grep. Run its status command. Run it after a cd . If any of those are refused, the self-protection rule is matching on words, and you will find out at a bad moment. Then try the opposite: a redirect into the hook's config, a sed -i on it, an edit that deletes its entry. Those should still be denied. A guard needs both halves to hold, or people turn it off. The code and the tests are in the repo: https://github.com/IgorGanapolsky/mac-yolo-safeguards

title: Free uncensored AI chat with no sign-up: how it works
author: UplinkSwitch
summary: Unrestrictable is an AI chat in the browser that runs open-weight models with the refusal behaviour removed or tuned out. You can try it with no account, nothing to install, and no card. This post explains what the free tier actually is, what is kept, and where the limits are. Figures are as the site stood on 2026-11-20. What "no sign-up" means here Open unrestrictable.ai/chat and type. There is no email field and no login; a human check stands in for the sign-in. Three free turns a day with no account. 239 models take those free turns, including GLM-5.3 Uncensored, DeepSeek V4 Pro Uncensored, GLM-5.3 Flash Abliterated, GLM-5.3 Flash Uncensored and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Abliterated. 385 of the site's 396 models are in the chat. The rest of them open with credit. The model picker sits in the composer. Each model is marked Free to try or With credit , and the free ones come first. You can switch models mid-conversation: the next reply comes from the one you picked and the earlier turns stay. What the models are The catalog is open-weight builds in three kinds: Abliterated: the refusal direction is removed from the weights. Uncensored: tuned without the filtering a general assistant ships with. Fiction-tuned: trained for long-form writing and roleplay. Every model gets the same test prompt daily and the result is public on the proof page ; on 2026-11-20, 310 of 338 checked models passed. What else the free chat does Files: attach a PDF, document or image up to 7 MB and it is read to text for the model. Web search: switch on Search the web and the reply cites the pages it found. Settings: a character, a system prompt and the temperature. Characters: 14 house characters, each a persona and an opening line. Every character is an adult. Voice input: the mic uses your browser's own speech recognition. A file or a search counts as one of the day's free turns. What is kept This is the part worth reading before you type anything personal. Your conversation is saved in your browser and nowhere else. Each turn is one request through the gateway, which keeps a usage record for billing: the model, the token counts and the charge. It does not store the prompt or the reply. The company running the model receives the request so it can answer. New messages are classified for safety by a moderation API; when it raises a flag, the categories are kept, never the text. With voice input, your browser's speech recognition may send the audio to the browser's maker; the site receives only the text. Memory , which stores notes on the server side, starts off. The privacy page lists every record. "Unrestricted" does not mean "no rules" The models answer without a stock refusal layer, so fiction can deal with dark subject matter and questions a filtered assistant declines get an answer. The acceptable use policy still applies to every request. It rules out, among other things, any sexual content involving minors, sexual content of a real person without their consent, attacking systems you are not authorized to test, and weapons of mass harm. On the image and video models, a prompt that describes a minor is refused before it reaches a model. When the free turns run out You will see a prompt for a key when today's free turns are used, the free budget is spent, or the model you picked runs on credit. Three options: A free account: 5 messages, 2 images and 3 files a day in the console chat, plus replies read aloud by a voice model, your own characters, a Create page for images, video, speech and music, and Memory if you switch it on. A top-up: a one-off payment from $10 by card, WeChat Pay, Alipay or crypto, with no ID and no phone number. 100 credits are $1, credits last 12 months, and each reply settles at that model's price per token on the pricing page . A usage plan that renews by card: Plus is $10 a month for $20 of usage, Pro $25 for $50, Max $100 for $200, Ultra $250 for $500. You can switch it off any time in Billing. Using the same models from code The chat is a front end on an API. The same models answer at an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible base URL, so SillyTavern, Cursor, Cline, OpenCode, Claude Code or the OpenAI SDK can use them with a key: export OPENAI_BASE_URL = "https://api.unrestrictable.ai/v1" export OPENAI_API_KEY = "your-key" Paste a key from the console into the chat and every model there opens as well. Try it unrestrictable.ai/chat : three turns, no account. The models page lists all 396 with their prices.

title: An LLM API for authorized pentesting: setup, scope, reporting
author: UplinkSwitch
summary: Most AI pentesting tools have two parts: an agent loop that runs commands, and a model that decides what the loop does next. The agent is usually open source and takes an OpenAI-compatible base URL. The model is the part that refuses. A general assistant often declines at the word "exploit" even when the target is in scope and the paperwork is signed, and an agent that hits a refusal mid-run stops or wanders. PentestLLM sells that second part: security-tuned, abliterated and uncensored open-weight builds on one prepaid key, for systems you own or have written permission to test. Prices are from the live catalog on 2026-11-20. Setup The API speaks the OpenAI and Anthropic wire formats, so any client that takes a base URL works: the OpenAI SDK, PentestGPT, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Cline, aider, or a Kali MCP client. Setting Value OpenAI-compatible base URL https://api.pentestllm.ai/v1 API key sk-ptl-... from the console Model auto/security , or a fixed id from the models page A first request: curl https://api.pentestllm.ai/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-ptl-live-..." \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "auto/security", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Rank these scanner findings by severity and say what to verify first."}] }' auto/security lets the router pick a fast, balanced or frontier security build per request, billed at that build's price with no router fee. Where a tool needs a fixed id, the setup guides use Gemma 4 26B A4B Cybersecurity ( gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-cybersecurity , 262,144 tokens of context), which takes tool calls. Choosing a build comes down to three things: Context window. A full scan export or a long source file needs room; the largest security build takes 1M tokens. Tool calling. An agent needs a build that takes tool calls; each model page lists the parameters it supports. Price. Agent work is mostly input, because every turn resends the conversation, the tool results and the files in view. Input prices for security builds start at $0.40 per million tokens. Agent setup pages: Claude Code , Cursor , Cline , OpenCode , and the rest under pentestllm.ai/guides . Where it fits in an engagement The model reads, ranks and drafts; the tester decides what runs. It works next to the tools you already use rather than replacing them: Burp Suite: paste or export a request, response or issue list and ask for a summary, a severity read or a retest note. Burp stays the tool that touches the target. Nuclei: feed the JSON results of a scan you ran in scope; the model groups duplicates, ranks by likely impact and lists what to confirm by hand. Proof of concept: it drafts a PoC for a confirmed finding, run first against your own lab copy of the target. Scope first Put the scope document and the rules of engagement where the agent can read them, at the top of the system prompt: the in-scope assets, the test window and any exclusions. Ask the model to point out notes that mention assets it cannot match to that list. It can miss one. Checking every action and every finding against the scope stays a human job. The key is for systems you own or are authorized in writing to test. Reduced refusals do not widen that. The acceptable use policy says a key may be suspended until proof of authorization is shown, and a signed engagement letter is that proof. Reporting Reporting is where a model saves the most time. From your notes it drafts: Findings: title, affected assets, description and the evidence you collected. Impact: what the issue means for this client, in plain terms. Remediation: a fix, a short-term mitigation and how to confirm the fix worked. Executive summary: one page for readers who will not open the technical section. Severity wording: it walks a CVSS vector with you and says which metrics are arguable. Two rules keep it honest: Redact before it leaves. Agree with the client what may go to an outside model. Most reporting work does not need real values: replace hostnames, IPs, user names and credentials with placeholders like HOST-01 or USER-A, keep the mapping locally, and restore the real values in the final document. On this API, request and response bodies are not retained by default; a key can opt in to seven days of retention for replay, which you should leave off for client work unless the client agrees. The reviewer signs, not the model. With thin notes, a model writes fluent text about things that did not happen. Treat every draft as a junior colleague's first pass, remove anything you did not observe, and confirm each CVSS vector yourself. Asking the model to mark each sentence it inferred rather than read from the notes makes review much faster. The full reporting walkthrough is at pentestllm.ai/use-cases/pentest-reporting .
